definition: A share is one small unit of ownership in a company, and its price changes as people trade it on a stock exchange.
A stock exchange is the official marketplace where shares are traded, with rules that companies and traders on it must follow.
An index is a single number that tracks the combined prices of a chosen group of shares, so it shows how the market as a whole moved.
A sector index tracks the combined prices of companies in one industry, such as banks or IT, so you can compare a stock with similar companies.
Market capitalisation is the total value the stock market puts on a company: its share price multiplied by the total number of its shares.
The P/E ratio is the share price divided by the profit per share over the last year, showing how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of profit.
The sector median P/E is the middle value of the P/E ratios of companies in the same industry, so half of them are higher and half are lower.
Earnings per share is a company's net profit for a period divided by the number of its shares, so it shows the profit behind each share.
Revenue is the total money a company earns from selling its products or services in a period, before any costs are taken out.
Net profit is the money left from revenue after all costs, interest and taxes are paid; if costs are larger, the result is a net loss.
Net margin is net profit as a percentage of revenue, so a 10% net margin means ₹10 of profit from every ₹100 of sales.
ROE (return on equity) is a year's net profit as a percentage of shareholders' money in the company, which is what it owns minus what it owes.
Debt to equity compares what a company has borrowed with shareholders' money in it, so a ratio of 2 means it owes ₹2 for every ₹1 of shareholders' money.
A promoter is the person, family or group that started or controls a company and usually owns a large part of its shares.
Promoter holding is the percentage of a company's shares that its promoters own, reported to the stock exchange every quarter.
Promoters pledge shares when they hand them to a lender as security for a loan; the lender can take the shares if the loan is not repaid.
An NBFC, or non-banking financial company, lends money like a bank but cannot offer savings or current accounts, so it mostly borrows from banks and investors.
Net interest income is the interest a bank or lender earns on its loans minus the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings.
Bad loans, or gross NPAs (non-performing assets), are loans whose borrowers have missed payments for more than 90 days, often shown as a percentage of all loans.
Quarterly results are the revenue, profit and other key figures a company reports to the stock exchange every three months.
A revenue outlook, also called guidance, is the company's own estimate of how much its revenue may grow over the coming year.
A dividend is a part of a company's profit paid out in cash to shareholders, usually stated as rupees per share.
A bonus issue gives existing shareholders extra free shares, so the share count goes up and the price per share drops, but the total value held stays the same.
A stock split divides each share into several smaller shares, so you hold more shares at a lower price each, and the total value does not change.
The ex-date is the first trading day on which shares bought no longer come with an announced dividend or bonus, so the quoted price usually adjusts that day.
The record date is the day a company checks its list of shareholders to decide who receives an announced dividend, bonus or split.
A corporate action is a company decision that changes what shareholders hold or receive, such as a dividend, bonus issue or stock split.
An upper circuit is the highest price the exchange allows a stock to reach in one day; at that price there are often many buyers and few sellers.
A lower circuit is the lowest price the exchange allows a stock to reach in one day; at that price there are often many sellers and few buyers.
Surveillance measures are extra rules an exchange puts on a stock with unusual price moves, such as asking traders to pay the full amount upfront.
A block deal is one large trade of a company's shares between big investors, done in a separate time slot and made public by the exchange.
Index inclusion is when a stock is added to an index, so funds that copy that index need to purchase its shares, usually around a set date.
Volatility measures how much a stock's price usually swings up and down; a higher number means bigger moves in both directions.
A drawdown is a fall in price from a previous high point to a later low point, shown as a percentage of the high.
A typical bad month is the 10th-percentile month: in the last three years, only about one month in ten was worse than this.
Annualised means a figure has been converted to a yearly rate, so numbers measured over different lengths of time can be compared fairly.
A trading session is one day the stock market is open for trading, so weekends and market holidays do not count.
A small-cap is a company with a small market capitalisation (total stock-market value); its shares often swing more and can be harder to trade in large amounts.
Liquidity is how easily you can trade a share without moving its price much; a share with few daily trades has low liquidity.
An exchange filing is an official statement a company sends to the stock exchange, such as its results, new orders or replies to exchange questions.
An AGM, or annual general meeting, is the yearly meeting where a company's shareholders vote on items such as the yearly accounts, dividends and directors.
Stale news is news older than 30 days; prices usually react to news within days, so old news rarely explains a recent move.
An adjusted price is a past price recalculated for a bonus issue or stock split, so the chart compares like with like across that date.
The 3-year growth rate is the steady yearly rate that would take a figure, such as revenue or profit, from its level three years ago to its level today.
